comments.text:
Everyone coming to this video complaining "f***** miners, let's kill them all!" yes, I agree. Kill them... in CSGO/COD/Battleshit II... but also, you need to recognise that they AREN'T the sole cause of the current GPU shortage. The real cause is AT LEAST 4-fold:

1) Supposed memory price fixing corruption is raising the price of memory, which adds significantly to GPU cost
2) Memory is in severe shortage due to mobile phone companies like Apple and Samsung (which use the same memory as most GPU's) gobbling up limited supplies of memory as they are manufactured, leaving the scraps for the gpu makers and other companies
3) Crypto-currency mining is causing normal people, underground illegal congregations and upstart companies to buy up every GPU powerful enough to mine efficiently, significantly increasing demand and reducing supply
4) Finally, ALL of the above pushes new PC gamers and people looking to build new systems no choice but to build systems with low spec GPU's, the demand for which also spikes big time, causing the price to rise for even the smaller cards too... 

And thus we have the perfect storm of GPU price gouging for 2018 and possibly onwards...

I know EXACTLY why video cards have been straying far above MSRP: cryptocurrency mining. You see, many cryptocurrency miners build homemade "mining rigs" out of several and several graphics cards. So, the reason graphics cards have been priced so far above MSRP is because a few cryptocurrency miners are snapping up graphics cards like crazy. http://www.pcgamer.com/what-you-need-to-know-about-cryptocurrency-mining/

By the way, I would NOT at all be surprised if some of the more avid cryptocurrency miners have been subject to false-alarm drug busts because their houses have consumed a great many more kilowatt-hours in any one month than the surrounding houses in their neighborhoods! So, why would excess electricity usage lead to a drug bust, anyway? Here's why: all U.S. power companies are in contact with the DEA (Drug Enforcement Agency). Each power company is required to report any households that are consuming electricity in excess to the DEA. The reason for THAT is marijuana grow ops. A house that contains a marijuana grow op pretty much always uses FAR more electricity each month than do the surrounding legitimate houses. This is mostly due to the grow lights that the marijuana plants require. The DEA will conduct a drug bust on any house that's found to be using electricity far in excess of the neighboring houses. Thus, I wouldn't be surprised if sometimes, instead of finding a basement or attic full of pot plants, DEA agents might find a basement full of rows of graphics cards (ie. a REALLY powerful cryptocurrency mining rig)! comments.text:
I mean, there's other reasons for the price difference, my main thought would be materials that are used on top of the reference card to make it cost more.  There are a lot of offerings that include "better" cooling solutions, so it makes sense that with higher quality materials, the price would jump up from MSRB.

The other issues is supply and demand.  Many of these cards are pretty much sold out when they hit the shelves, so the pricing could go up if demand is high for them.  You could argue that as consumers, we could stop paying so much for so little, and you would be right, and I myself have picked out a nice card from MSI/NVIDIA that has a good cooler (Sea Hawk X, has a Corsair water cooler attached).  This is also after waiting almost 6 years before upgrading to a new computer, mind you.

If everyone in the world stopped paying over $500 for the most premium products out there, then yes, hardware companies will have no choice but to drop the pricing.  As it is, consumers are pushing for these prices with their wallets, and no business is gonna say no to that, so the issue will continue until it becomes unanimously accepted across all markets.

Last note, how could you not think about hot-swapping computer fans?  That's the dream, right there.

comments.text:
- First of all you need to find a spare fan. 
- Remove the fan from the card if you can pop it out like this one.
- Pull the sticker off the front of the fan blades to see the axle and bearing and stuff.
- There will be some kind of clip to hold the blades in. Some have a plastic ring, others have a metal c-clip.
- Remove the clip and pull the blades out (you will need a really small tool for this. I used a tiny flat head screwdriver attachment for my small screwdriver. A tiny pick would work better. If it uses a c-clip you're going to have to pry it apart to get it out of the recess on the axle. Good luck with that. lol
- Don't lose the spring on the back of the fan that holds it all up.
- - Since you have the fan blades out i go ahead and add a drop of marvel mystery oil on the axle.
- Slap the new fan in there with the spring, replace the clip, pop it back in the case or whatever was holding it and you should be good to go.

If you wanted to (or did) clip the wires on the back of the fan assembly you should solder them back together with a small soldering iron and protect the connection with a heat shrink wrap. Remember to slide the heat shrink wrap on first, solder, then shrink the wrap over your solder. ;)

That should be everything you need to know. I just replaced a CPU cooler's fan blades the other day.

comments.text:
When you've got most of the market cornered you could base your pricing off of fairy dust.

There really isn't any competition in the area of graphics cards anymore.  Remember the mid 80's to mid 90's? There were many more companies in the game. Now it's pretty much AMD or NVidia, at least for most standard consume cards and even some pro/prosumer cards.

The various Quadro cards for example  They are essentially cherry picked print outs of the best cards in a batch with more memory and different firmware.  They cost many times more not because they cost that much more to produce but "because they can"  There's not enough competition to keep them from doing so.

ATI was actually doing a fairly good job of being competition until they were purchased by AMD. And AMD in turn was doing okay in the CPU space for a while. And then they decided to just start shitting the bed as hard as they possibly could.

Think back for just a minute and you'll actually remember a time when you'd hear a friend talk about building a new computer with an ATI (not AMD) Radeon with an AMD whateverthehell CPU (their naming scheme has always been stupid).

Think back even farther and you'll remember a time where one of your friends actually had a 3DFX Voodoo card, and it was actually pretty good (for the time).

I have to say that even with that big difference between MSRP and actual price, It seems like AMD might have finally stopped shitting the bed and started to clean up the mess. because the first time since i finished high school (about 17 years ago); I am actually seriously considering a fully AMD based system. comments.text:
I run an old X58 system and upgraded my i7 920 to an X5670. I have been running an AMD 5870 since they came out and it has been great except in the last 12 months with games like The Division and GTA V it was clearly time to upgrade. I was so excited to see the pre launch pricing from both Red and Green. I am not a fan boy but simply want the best bang for buck at any given time.
I was going to go for a 480 8gb but the pricing was getting towards £300 in the UK and not many non reference versions available. The GTX 1060 was about the same. If I looked at 1070's then the card I wanted were £450 plus.
Then came across an offer for a Zotac GTX 980ti AMP Extreme. OK so on spec's it uses more power and is hotter than nVidia's current offering (neither of which bother me) but if you take gaming, editing, encoding into the picture plus a 5 year warranty (remember how long I have had my 5870) and for just a bit more than the 480 or 1060 and at least £100 less than a 1070 it became an easy choice for me for a top spec and quality GPU. 
I game at 1080p and this is more card than I need and will fit into my next system which I hope to purchase in the next 12 months. It might be new or 2nd hand. As ever I will build it myself and reuse as much as possible but depending on what Zen looks like and the pricing it might be my first AMD CPU (or another used Xeon setup).

comments.text:
***** A quad-core cpu and GTX 1050ti can easily be powered by a 430w power supply. If you leeway for upgrades, 500w is the most you should ever go. A gold-certified is absolutely overkill, unless you're planning to keep your pc on literally 24/7. Even then, there's not much difference between a silver certified and a gold certified psu. It's nice to have a super good quality supply and one with high watts, but going into abundance territory is a luxury you simply cannot afford in a build where you're still using a rather entry-level graphics card. 

The 500 SSD is stupid. You're not going to be constantly using 500GB of storage. Get a 240gb SSD at most and pair it with an actual hard drive (which are really cheap). 

The mastercase is even stupider, cut down its price by half and you're still able to buy some really nice cases like a Corsair 200R.

With this money you saved, a 1070 is easily fit into a $1000 budget.

comments.text:
What's wrong with GPU pricing right now in a nutshell:

-GTX 780 & 770 introduce a new reference blower design that for the first time ever doesn't look and perform like crap. This creates an interesting value proposition for people who either prefer the thermal characteristics of blower coolers or who want an attractive card without paying the aftermarket premium. Why buy the shitty plastic blowers when the reference cooler is better looking, better performing, and often still comes at MSRP?
-Said reference designs are quickly phased out for aftermarket offerings, creating a situation where reference coolers are both hard to find and desirable, which drives up value. Cue people willing to pay an extra premium to get the GOOD, reference blowers because nobody wants a shitty slab of whining plastic in their case.
-This trend continues for the 900 series, and Nvidia takes notice that there's a demand for their nicely-designed reference coolers, and a market segment willing to buy them at a premium.
-Nvidia comes up with a fancy idea: Reference coolers that are available for the lifetime of the product. However, this creates a new problem: Nvidia can't price their board partners out of a market segment (e.g. they'll sell for a premium but they don't want to price them low enough to compete with the aftermarket offerings), and conversely the board partners can't then offer a reference cooled version that competes with Nvidia's to beat their version.
-The solution to this problem? Screw it, just price the damn thing right up there with the best cards! Introducing the FOUNDER'S EDITION.

So now we have no reference blowers to sell at MSRP, nobody wants the shitty plastic blowers that perform like crap and look like crap so no board partners are making them, and so all we're seeing are the premium-priced aftermarket offerings and then the premium-priced Founder's Edition cards.

Similarly AMD's reference cards aren't all that desirable, so most of what you're seeing from them is also aftermarket, though their reference designs are selling for MSRP and thus getting bought up pretty quickly as well as being phased out (as board partners have always done).

Thankfully as happened in previous years board partner designs will eventually come down to MSRP, and as long as founder's edition sales haven't been through the roof (They probably have been unfortunately), we might see Nvidia take some measure to keep their reference designs available WITHOUT pricing them through the roof and simply let market demand dictate the price segment.

Hey, my family runs a media creation company so i can give u real advice.
For video editing, you have 2 options, go with cpu or gpu. If you are going cpu, the newer 6xxx series are not much powerful than the 4790k (comparing the price vs performance). If you choose to go the gpu route, the newer gtx's are basically handicaped in the area of video editing(renders effects slower). The sensible option for me was to buy a i5 4690k with a gtx 660ti. i know its a older card but performs much better than the 750ti while rendering(comparing relative to price as i was on a budget). other options are nvidia's tesla(breaks the bank) or quadro(cheaper) series cards which cost a shit ton and are better suited for 3d workloads. The best i found which in relation to cost were the 6xx series from nvidia, however they aren't available in the new product market and rare in the used. Your best bet if on a budget is getting 

i7 4790k + cooler master hyper 212 evo cooler
32 gigs kingston hyperX fury ram 1866(budget) or 2133(negligible cost diff)
gigabyte ud5h black edition(important u get the black ed.)
corsair rm650 psu (a premium, silent and non-bankBreaker psu)
and maybe couple of hdds in a raid 0 array or a ssd(or multiple)

and waiting till you have the money to buy a mainstream video editing card (amd w5000 is a great vfm), but if you are learning or rendering a 30 minute video with moderatly heavy effects everyday, you maybe happy with the above system+ a watercooler(h100i).



happy to help further

777Mikos , Yes it would as speed is always good, GPGPU or not.

When playing games, you dont tend to care about the render quality. GPGPU (the component i raved about), doesnt let this happen. When they removed it and sped up the cuda cores, the performance increased but the quality went down. When Antares 8001 mentioned the comparison between his 570 and 1080 and it turned out to only 5%, it means that the gpu has to repeatedly render the sequence to reach acceptable quality and then push it out or render it slower ensuring quality. In my research, if ur gonna go for a card of that price range, you might as well get a amd card as the raw compute( OpenCL or DirectCompute) power of amd cards directly relate to their gaming performance as it doesnt have these "fake" features to dramatically increase gaming performance while fucking up the quality of the rendered sequence. ati 7xxx would be be best for you with 7770 by saphire being the best vfm.

Amd cards being hot(af), i recommend getting a waterblock for the card and hookup a custom or premade watercooling solution. JaysTwoCents has a great build vlog which he did for his personal computer from which you can take tips or just follow the whole tut and you will have not only better cooling, but also way better performance as the processor heats up it looses quality and performance(even if running at the same frequency).

+simons700 I love "TL;DR" reviews. 

I don't give a flying shit about the performance in 50 billion different titles. There's more than enough graphs for that somewhere else. A review, for me, should get to the point. The card either performs well across a small number of tested titles or it doesn't. Adding more games to the mix is not always a good thing. The games they test are well optimized, and have been out for a while so driver support is available. This "levels the playing field".

Those benchmarks aren't even there to show people that the game will run at X FPS on THEIR GPU, they're meant to show the DIFFERENCE between GPU's. Each PC is slightly different, so performance won't ever be comparable with benchmarks anyway. They help people choose a new GPU. "This card, on average, performs better than this card"

And forza, seriously? That's another one of those Xone ports. They aren't to be trusted. That's like benchmarking fucking batman:AK, it makes no sense because it isn't optimised properly (Yet, or at least we don't know that.), which results in quirky shit like some architectures performing worse for no good reason.

Benjus Maximus Well gaming is an expensive hobby, it is by no means a cheap hobby. If people want 30 fps at $100 that's fine by them, but don't complain that you're basically getting ripped off, when you can have 90 or 200 FPS for double the price. The RX 470 is the best price for performance GPU on the market, and if people are too dumb to realise that and they purchase the inferior and overpriced RX 460 then so be it. But they are literally an idiot. 

Mind you this RX 460 model requires a PSU with a power connector anyway, so if you don't have a PSU with a power connector you have to spill extra cash anyway.

Nothing about the RX 460 makes any sense, if an eSports gamer who wants to spend as little money as possible wants to purchase a graphics card something like the 750 Ti makes more sense. You can find a used 750 Ti no problems cheaper than a RX 460. Most if not all 750 TI models, require no power connector, and most eSports games don't use more than a 1 GB of VRAM, you are literally spending extra money on 4GB of VRAM. On top of that the 750 Ti delivers reasonable performance compared to the RX 460 and will be able to play many eSports titles no problems above 60 FPS, and DX12 isn't even a factor for games like LOL, DoTA 2, CS:GO and Overwatch...

I fail to see why anyone would buy an RX 460, because if you want that level of performance there are cheaper options available, they don't have to purchase a power supply like they would this card and they don't need DX 12 or extra fancy features to play the titles they are geared towards.

The pricing within AMD's own cards are completely fucked, I mean for a start if they were selling at MSRP again the 470 is $30 more than the 460. I mean c'mon you're telling if the MSRP were real that people wouldn't purchase the RX 470 for an extra $30? I highly doubt that.

I'm just arguing the 470 is the reasonable and best value deal for budget video cards right now, as it delivers the best bang for buck. PC Gaming is not cheap and if people truly want a level playing ground for competitive games at a cheap price then they should move to consoles where the hardware is the same and performance is equal for everyone.

Lastly, the fact anyone thinks they are going to get a good gaming experience at $100 is ridiculous, I know that if I buy a $10 microphone from the dollar store that it won't sound anything like an $80 microphone from a music shop. But the quality of that $80 microphone is the most reasonable, sure I may pay 400% more than I did at the dollar store, but the quality sounds much much better. As long as people can hear my voice reasonably clear with little static and interference, then the $80 microphone is the best value. Not the fucking microphone from the dollar store, and certainly I don't want the person to shell out for a $900 microphone...

Your argument is stupid, purely because if someone wants good value gaming then consoles are the best option not an RX 460.

My argument is logical, which is okay you want to do PC gaming, well it's going to cost you, not a lot, but quite a bit and here's the best valued options with the best performance. Enjoy 1080p 60 FPS on pretty much every modern title with High settings with the RX 470 or be confined to subpar 30 FPS on the RX 460 if you're lucky. Your call, but if you want 200 FPS at 1080p on CS:GO for your 144 HZ monitor, then the 470 is the best product since the 460 can't achieve that.

comments.text:
Raavi Mehta

It is never undesirable for a graphics card (not GPU) to be power efficient because it also allows a higher performance. The bottleneck for graphics cards often is that they get too hot because they have a high electrical power. I'll start with some general explanation which you might appreciate given that you are new to this, in the last paragraph I'll answer your question, you interpret that comment in the wrong way. In engineering it always is about making tradeoffs, you can choose between a lot of points on multidimensional axes and somewhere you get a desired optimum between price, performance, efficiency etcetera.
In the case of AMD cards of the last generations there has been a trend to more parallellism. All graphics cards are strongly paralllized processors (the difference with CPU's which are much less parallized but which do excell with a much higher clockspeed) but AMD cards have a much better capability to run more different processes in pararllel. This gives AMD cards the edge in DX12 and Vulkan and it decrease the idel time but it also gives more overhead in DX11 (much more CPU overhead) and it gives them a higher wattage. There is no good or bad choice here, AMD antcipated the modern API's and AMD has built the foundation for it with Mantle which Khronos Group used to develop Vulkan and which Microsoft used to develop DX12. At this moment AMD gets rewarded for this with better DX12 and Vulkan performance but it looses terrain on DX11 performance.
Regardless of that NVidia did also develop a very efficient driver for DX11 and a very power  efficient architecture for the 900 series cards and the 1000 series cards. Basicallly you should make your choice between NVidia and AMD for the coming time based upon this:

- do you want FreeSycn/G-Sync? If so, for G-Sync monitors you pay 100-200 euro more while both technologies give almost (negligible) the same performance. Basically FreeSync and G-Sync prevent tearing while not increasing the input lag. If you don't understand this, ask and I'll explain.

- do you find the performance in future games more important of do you find the performance in existing DX11 games more important?

Other than that you should know that you can't use two 1060 cards but you can use two 480 cards.

In the original comment he didn't complain about the fact that this card is "power efficient". Actually, that is not well phrased, what he meant is that the card has a low wattage, that is not the same. His complaint was that they put extra ventilators, heat pipes and an extra power connector on this card because it increases the price while it doesn't add that much value. I disagree to some extend. You shouldn't need the extra power connector if you have a proper motherboard but it does increase the clockspeed a bit, at the cost of much extra power (not efficient). I value good ventilators because they give less noise. A bigger problem in my opinion is that the heatpipes do not overlap the GPU and the RAM, probably because they don't want to design one for ervery card because this is cheaper.

Rene Hourian 144hz is getting to the point of almost no gains in technical performance over lower refresh rates.

i know that 144hz is alot smoother and very helpfull for competitive games, but going above that doesn't really help as you are either getting screen tearing or reintroducing the input lagg you tried so hard to remove by going from 60hz to 144hz.

if CS:GO only draws full frames in order to remove any kind of frame-lagg, then going above 144hz just introduces more frame-lagg and inconsistencies. 

when playing at 144fps with a 144hz screen then the time between each refresh is equal to the time between each available frame.

by adding more frames means that the screen will only rarely hit the optimal frametime and it will have to wait for the next frame in most occations. 

let's take a hypotheical scenario here.

you make a food that has a protein that tastes horrible after 1 minute and the food will taste worse and worse by the second.

you have a machine that automaticly makes 1 pr. minute.

if you eat it when it comes out every minute then you get the optimal experience where the taste it perfect.

let's say you can now only eat 1 portion every 1:50 minutes. 

you eat the first portion and wait till you can eat again. now you are faced with the fact that the meal that is ready right now will taste close to horrible or you would have to wait for 10 seconds before you can eat a perfect meal again.


that is essentially what happens with frames in CS:GO. if it's like what you guys proclaim and that the engine only picks out full frames and not the readily available frames, then it will most of the time be outdated frames if you go higher than your refreshrate. if you have your framerate locked tot he same speed of the refreshrate you will get the best experience. you get the speed that your monitor is capable off and you get essentially 0 input and display lagg.

the comment that CS:GO's input is tied to framerate is just bullshit as no sane developer would make that horrible game mechanic. the input is computed seperately from the what you see visually. you techicly move before you see it on screen. 

the difference in movement to visual is just so small that most people won't notice it immidiately. it's a matter of milliseconds.

comments.text: Rene, screen tearing has nothing to do with the Source engine, no game engine generates anything other than full frames on the GPU. Screen tearing occurs on the framebuffer when a new frame is pushed to the buffer while the previous one is still being drawn by the monitor. comments.text: Try the CSGO benchmark, its in the workshop, because it turns that varience into a frame time counter instead. Which is interesting to see too. At 999fps frame times are around 0.9ms. Meaning a new frame is produced every 0.9ms. Within a given refresh that gives the game normally 5 frames to pick from to display as the most recent frame at 144hz. Without syncing, the more frames you produce within a refresh cycle if a monitor, the more likely that frame shown will be the most recently rendered and with more consistentency. ﻿If you're at 144fps exactly, what happens is you begin to get out of sync frames that might have been rendered up to ~5ms before the refresh of the monitor.

Now if you double, or tripple, or quadruple your blinkers rate, the number of times that match up happens is more frequent. Even if it isn't an exact doubling.
